### 2026-10-06 – # Oct 5: Planning and first work in KiCad

**9h**

# Oct 5: Planning and first work in KiCad
After coming up with my project concept, I first decided to make a list of the parts I would work with and features I would want. I already have a FNIRSI GC-01 Geiger Counter, so I have a good reference of readings and problems with it. The readings often jump a lot at low radiation levels (background) and there is no Wi-Fi functionality. So I've decided my Geiger will support Wi-Fi ([ESP32-C3](https://documentation.espressif.com/esp32-c3_datasheet_en.pdf))  and use a SBM-20 tube (quite a bit bigger than the M4011 in the FNIRSI and should be more reliable). On top of the ESP and the tube, I will need a high voltage supply which I will design and some other smaller electronics (like a buzzer for impulses and a USB-C port for charging).

The SBM-20 tube needs about 400 volts to operate (see [datasheet](https://www.gstube.com/data/2398/)), which is quite scary, considering we are starting with 3.3 Volts. I researched some ways to get there, and although I was considering making a simple straight boost converter (single inductor all the way to 400V), I decided to go with something called a [Cockcroft-Walton voltage multiplier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cockcroft%E2%80%93Walton_generator). It's a bit more efficient on the components, as the inductor only needs around 130 Volts (we can use cheaper caps rated for lower voltage) and the chain of diodes and capacitators will triple it, reaching our desired 400 volts.

After getting a rough idea of the whole project structure, I decided to install KiCad. I didn't have much experience, so I spent the first few minutes just looking around and figuring out the basics controls. After making the project, I was able to find the specific components I would use on [lscs](https://www.lcsc.com/) and imported them into KiCad (notably the USB-C port, ESP32 and so on).

Here's my finished LCSC cart (after the schematic was done):
![Finished LCSC cart](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/065e70f69a7e693ca2c8ea7365e14bee4707386e6e35ef32793546f8197218ce.png)

After looking around, I was still a bit worried about the High Voltage part of the project, so I decided to sketch out the Cockcroft-Walton multiplier on paper. I was a bit confused about the orientation of some components, but later figured it out after a few attempts.

![My attempt at a Cockcroft-Walton multiplier](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/8b515fa07cf62735a4b51d7d8cfe81bb46daaa292e8e4817a2693815881eb36c.jpg)

Next, it was time to actually lay stuff down in KiCad. So I started with the power section, as our Geiger wil certainly not work without power. After doing a bit of research into USB-C connectors, I realized the USB-C connector needs 5.1 kiloohm pulldown resistors on the CC pins, so I made a simple charging circuit in KiCad:

![USB-C and TP4056 charging circuit](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/1f528be8d5d1feb5c5bc4b05358a16bb2f015275e1bc77326ef88cb5764cc90b.png)

**Next up:** The hardest part of the project, high voltage circuit.

**tl;dr: Picked out components, setup and learned KiCAD basics, drafted high voltage circuit, made basic charging circuit**

**In total, the time spent doing research, assembling part lists, drawing the circuits and creating the charging circuit was 3 hours.**

# Oct 6: High voltage supply
This was definitely the hardest part of the entire schematic. I picked the MMBTA42 transistor, which switches the inductor via PWM from the ESP32. When it switches off, the energy of the inductor goes through the first diode and the multiplier chain steps it up step by step.

![Multiplier chain of the HV circuit](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/dab66825c64f244c42a72dc34f70ce0875fb1143ecb81ce2ef5cb4cec305493c.png)

A problem I didn't expect was the feedback divider. I need to bring down 400V down to something the ESP32 can handle. I thought of using a simple voltage divider, but the top resistor would need to be around 100 megaohms, and I quickly figured out that a simple 0805 resistor is rated only for 150 volts. So I decided to put 10 10megaohm resistors in a series to spread the voltage. The bottom one is 220k, which gives a ratio of about 455:1, leading to only 0.88V on the ESP32's ADC.

![Feedback divider](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/d15ea0c232001be456ae95da6db0bdc8adafced1c7943e9f0d74405f992861b0.png)

When the board is off, the divider also slowly drains the HV capacitors through 100 megaohms, so that the user doesn't get shocked handling the board afterwards.

![Finished HV circuit](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/2e39d99808e3751c83391b4cc886b922f4f97be053c2340232a688e557db6dad.png)

**Next up:** Wiring the ESP32 and detecting radioactive impulses.

**tl;dr: Built the high voltage circuit stepping up to 400 volts.**

**Total time spent: ~2.5 hours**

# Oct 6: ESP32 wiring and pulse detection
It was a bit tricky getting the pin assignment on the ESP32 right. I needed to check the datasheet to figure out which support ADC and which do PWM.
![ESP32 wiring](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/d009ecc4050545c63832173b4ea8af743bfdd0ba9356588aa2ce88198ac12878.png)

The SBM-20 tube connects through a 2-pin header. The anode of the tube gets around 400V through a 4.7megaohm resistor, which limits the current to about 85 microampers. When a radioactive decay event is detected, a particle ionizes the gas inside the SBM-20 tube and the tube conducts briefly, causing the cathode to drop. An MMBT3904 transistor is used to invert that into a clean signal for the ESP32.

The buzzer uses another MMBT3904 transistor as a switch. I had to add a 10kiloohm pulldown resistor on the base because the pins of the ESP32 can float during boot and the buzzer could make random noises as it boots. I also added a flyback diode across the buzzer, so when the transistor switches off it kicks back a voltage spike, and the diode gives it somewhere to go.
![Buzzer and pulse detection area](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/472ccab77308b63ae3383ea122e2d8787ab7f7f6333403b5fb41eb123449cccd.png)

**Next up:** Final checks and safety

**tl;dr: Setup the wiring for the SBM-20 Geiger tube and added pulse detection, added the buzzer for detecting impulses**

**Total time spent: ~2 hours**

# Oct 6: Protection circuits and final checks
To finish the schematic, I added ESD protection (USBLC6-2) on the USB data lines to make sure that static from plugging a cable cannot kill the ESP32. Another diode on the VBUS handles voltage spikes from bad chargers.
![Protection circuits](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/b0d6fd8d3b877b3af5de3616bec333c08f65ec431d53d3e3138bd82b806f1078.png)

To finalize my schematic, I ran the Electrical Rules Checker in KiCad, which came back without errors.

![Passing ERC](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/b2f598b2d6cc2c22a52ea00944b3a08f631c0c3bfee2532510714ebc36e3d563.png)

Final schematic:

![Final schematic](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/ff7017ac22739afb2a1fe34a2edd118645c38f1584eb66f966ff99527dccb93f.png)

**Next up:** Footprint assignment and starting the PCB layout

**tl;dr: Added ESD and overvoltage protection, schematic passes ERC. Schematic is done.**

### 2026-10-06 – # Oct 6: Footprint assignment

**1.5h**

# Oct 6: Footprint assignment

After my schematic was finished, I decided to begin the necessary work before I could actually start designing the PCB itself. The first step was assigning physical footprints to each component in my schematic, as KiCAD needs to know how big each resistor, capacitor and all the other components are.

Given that many of my components were imported from LCSC, they already had a lot of footprints, but most of the passive components (resistors, capacitors and diodes) needed me to manually assign them.

For the resistors, I picked the 0805 resistor as it is small enough, but can still be soldered by hand. Parts of the HV circuit needed different resistors though, notably the feedback divider, as 0805 is only rated for 150 Volts. I picked the 1206, as it is rated higher and is a similar size to the 0805.
![Assigned footprints](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/a5f5d4b15ad512da2b556de1f6d7934a916dac7b3ddb9a994e484bd40ba06f0b.png)

Diodes were a bit more confusing, but I ended up choosing SOD-123, SOD-123F and SOD-323. The buzzer was the biggest problem, as my model wasn't in the library. Ended up choosing the closest one, which was a Murata 9x9 buzzer, should be relatively close to the real one.

After assigning all footprints, I opened the PCB Editor for the first time, where I was quickly greeted with a huge mess. But that's a problem for tomorrow!

![Tomorrow's problems](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/9e7b4849c3c6b3cbedd3b5f45ba372223302c4b9e883d01948cd0d0c593a2f21.png)

**Next up:** PCB outline and component placement

**tl;dr: Added footprints to all components, imported my schematic in the PCB editor.**

**Total time spent: ~1.5 hours**

### 2026-10-07 – # Oct 7: PCB layout: placement and first routing

**3h**

# Oct 7: PCB layout: placement and first routing

Today, I started the actual layout of the PCB. First, I setup the board outline to be 90x50mm and started placed components. On the left, I put USB-C and charging related components. On the top right, I put the battery and LDO. I decided to put the ESP32 in the center of the board with its antenna pointing down, and I isolated the entire High Voltage circuit on the right with a bigger gap from everything else.

![The board with all components placed](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/6627c07e03f0d2982010b6dd56ed8ce6b256d1e01aa272464fa4e3dd17b1fe1e.png)

The SBM-20 tube will mount externally through our 2-pin header. Given the tube is 108mm long, it cannot fit on the board. This may be an advantage though, as you can point it at any surface or material freely.

Afterwards, I decided to configure design rules for safety. I made a special net class for the high voltage circuit with 6mm clearance to make sure that traces do not arc across the board at 400V.

![Configured net classes](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/c6b026f0288da666f96bef0d141f9a436f27e4ff27df03511c1b0b9d0055db15.png)

To finish the work for the day, I started work on the routing. I mostly familiarized myself with how it works, and tried routing the basics of the HV circuit, but it is only a rough sketch for now and will need a lot more work.

![Absolute basics of routing in the HV circuit](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/e098f8bf616ee322bedbd856b6f192bfb4ba31bcb9159a33eedd6f976b7bd172.png)

**Next up:** Finishing routing the board.

**tl;dr: Components placed on the actual PCB, design rules set, began work on learning how to route.**

**Total time spent: ~3 hours**

### 2026-10-08 – # Oct 8: Routing the board

**3.5h**

# Oct 8: Routing the board

I started properly working on the routing today. At the start, it was really rough. Yesterday, I started with the HV section. However, I quickly realized this is super challenging. I had no idea how to arrange the routes for it all to fit. I would just choose a pad, press X and start routing, but quickly ran out of space and paths for the traces to go.

![Traces from yesterday in the HV section](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/bf53db1fc00e919f9c867435502aa4ae66021e64993a5e383de8d5b05c7a2cfb.png)

I decided it would be a good idea to take a breather and try working on an easier section than HV. So I decided the USB-C section could be a good idea. I immediately ran into issues though. The pin spacing on the connector was so tight that my traces violated the spacing rules. I could not connect any pins of the port itself. At the very least, I tried routing the nearby components, which proved to be less of a challenge.

![USB-C section](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/ac4285e47934d91a922a765836dd1de7290ac2d48c6647862cab79cc505ae7a5.png)

After wiring a few things here, I decided to move to the middle, more notably the pins of the ESP32 and surrounding components (e.g. buzzer circuit). However, I quickly got a lot more frustrated when I realized there was no way I was gonna fit the traces. What was I meant to do? Rearrange everything? I was desperate and almost resorted to cheating, as I thought this must be a problem someone solved and looked for software that could auto route circuits. However, I felt it was unfair and after all, I was here to learn, so I tried looking for ways to properly route it. With just 5 minutes of exploring the editor, I made a massive revelation. **There are two layers!** Turns out, sometimes it's a good idea to approach problems with some problem-solving skill instead of slaving away at impossible tracing. I ended up fixing a few of my poor traces from when I assumed there was only one layer, and I started with routing the rest of the board, this time much more quicker.

I wired up the ESP32 layer, but later realized I made a mistake at the bottom, when I ran a trace through the bottom of it, where the antenna supposedly sits. This could cause major issues for the ESP32, and so I had to redo that trace, which was thankfully very simple with layer switching.

![ESP32 antenna wiring mistake](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/8c5dca672ecfec64c25bcc8fb56950b93b5c7939db17441a721666554e54d479.png)

Now, I'll be honest. My tracing is nowhere near exemplary, but I still am very proud of the fact that it is getting to a functional state.

![Today's routing progress](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/cd071a915ff7e469ba1c689aae64976c8c462c49da52566e4e8a3d2b056a32de.png)

Near the end, I realized another fatal mistake I made near the start. Given that we are working with 400V in the HV section, it is possible for a spark to arc through the board between individual traces (my classmate warned me of that, thanks!). As such, we need to follow clearance rules (I set a 6mm rule to have some headroom). Tomorrow, I will try to have another crack at finishing the USB-C section (I still haven't figured out how to properly connect the pins), fix the HV clearance and overall get routing finished.

**Next up:** Fixing the clearance violations, finishing remaining traces

**tl;dr: Discovered that the PCB has multiple layers, which was a game changer. Most of the board is now routed but a couple traces need rerouting as they carry high voltage and are too close.**

**Total time spent: ~3.5 hours**

### 2026-10-11 – #  Oct 9 - DRC fixes and ground pour

**8h**

#  Oct 9 - DRC fixes and ground pour

After finishing routing and rerouting a significant portion of the HV section, I ran the Design Rules Checker, only to be greeted with 111 errors. A lot of these were clearance errors from the USB-C port, which I intentionally left to overhang the PCB a little bit and the pins were too close to each other.

![Initial DRC errors](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/3aa037051bcaaa216a403b43252923e3029790ad5f944002b355807e8b47bbe1.png)

Fixing the USB-C errors was quite tricky, I tried a lot of ways, including extending the board edge and adding clearance rules, but later realized they were simply a part of the connector footprint and I could just exclude them. As such, I ended up excluding the issues from DRC, as supposedly these issues are not a problem and not my fault either.

Next steps were the copper ground pours on both layers. After filling the front and back layer with copper, several GND pads were still cut off from the main pour by surrounding traces, so I placed vias to connect them through the back layer, and I connected a few GND pads together.

![Missing GND connections after the ground pour](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/6ccc4c6454dcc33cf773baa805b5b0e8c46a378a11f0322488d822187be6337b.png)

After connecting all the GNDs properly, I was only met with a few warnings, and they were generally cosmetic and safe to ignore.

![preview](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/cc0cb2a94f16b92c99b3b0b694efad509e3bef62f582fd9246015767e2d07ad4.png)

After hours of redoing routing, fixing up 111 DRC errors and pouring copper, I finally had a proper 3D render of my PCB, and the PCB was done!

![Final rendered PCB](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/10c247f57ad7e5d44db99650c0275d253508ab703072a97e5148f1ba1a442e0e.png)

**Next up:** Finalizing the BOM and manufacturing files.

**tl;dr: Redid HV routing, fixed all DRC violations, added ground pour on both
layers, board passes all electrical checks.**

**Total time spent: ~4 hours**

# Oct 10: BOM, Gerbers and manufacturing prep

After all the routing was done, I exported the Gerber files and the drill files for JLCPCB. Uploaded them to JLCPCB and got a quote of 4$ for 5 bare PCBs, around 17$ with shipping to the Czech Republic.

I also tried configuring PCBA (having JLCPCB solder the components), but the price was astronomical, over 100$ because of extended component fees. Way over my budget. I'll have to hand solder everything during build week instead, which I'm quite nervous about.

![JLCPCB quote](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/f533d8d1dd6405e81e0fb99242464e1a63df50fc2e2588624e40e223180a72b9.png)

Building the BOM took way longer than I expected. I went through every component on LCSC, added them to the cart one by one and checked that each part number matched. And it's a really good thing I did, because two of the parts were wrong. Instead of the 10 megaohm resistor for the feedback divider, my cart had a 1 megaohm resistor from a different package, and the 10 nanofarad 1kV capacitor had been replaced by a 1 microfarad. It would have been quite catastrophic if I blindly ordered them, so I went through each part individually to make sure that everything was right.

![LCSC cart](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/cb209c83622ca114ae4f5ef610a874c422b2b80819fc593c25c2b36d1e6d5c6b.png)

Unfortunately, even with cost saving at every step, I ran into a huge issue. I was still way over budget. If I added the Geiger Tube and the battery that my PCB needed, I would approach 100$ instead of my 65$ budget. Thankfully, I have a Geiger counter at home, so I decided I will desolder the M4011 tube from it (it should be very similar to the SBM-20 I originally picked) and also reuse the battery, which is esentially exactly what I need. That way, I can save about 40$.

![Salvageable Geiger Tube and battery](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/a4b20bf4437d29b7b40cfa0bf026214b42fa50a72561b84c46bd3ef5f02f9c54.jpg)

**Next up:** Firmware and submission

**tl;dr: Exported Gerbers, built and verified the full BOM, total project cost around 55$.**

**Total time spent: ~2.5 hours**

# Oct 11: Firmware

I decided to write the firmware in MicroPython, as the ESP32 supports it natively and I already know it from school.

I wrote five modules for the firmware, hv_control.py which reads the HV feedback voltage and adjusts the PWM duty cycle to keep the HV output around 400 volts, geiger.py which counts pulses from the tube, buzzer.py which plays a short click on the buzzer on each pulse and an alarm tone for high radiation, wifi_manager.py which handles Wi-Fi connections a dashboard and main.py which controls the whole firmware.

I was a bit worried about it, but the code makes sense to me and I think there are no issues on it. I can't sadly test it until the board is fully built, but the pin assignments match and the logic seems accurate.

![Code preview](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/a379f6b637a62d678505ee4bdfb15295587619ceff5fcc0ccee068977464203d.png)

![Web dashboard](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/0goZLgWsbHGszBXR3vrqmdWCKeLzVap1/5e1f961ad1e40fb00775c8925f7f61d24620c8f5bf5cb993d3b8068f7ec91473.png)

**Next up:** Build week

**tl;dr: Full firmware in MicroPython with HV regulation, pulse counting, buzzer and a Wi-Fi dashboard.**

**Total time spent: ~1.5 hours**
